one_liner: RocksDB 5.18 fork that moves L0 into Optane persistent memory with fine-grained column compaction; 3.6x NVM-assisted RocksDB random-write throughput.
what_it_does: MatrixKV is the RocksDB v5.18.3 source tree with L0 moved off the SSD onto byte-addressable persistent memory (Intel Optane DC PMM, accessed through PMDK's libpmem) and reorganized so that the L0-to-L1 compactions behind write stalls become small and frequent. It targets write-heavy LSM workloads on a DRAM/NVM/SSD machine. The API is RocksDB's own: you build this tree in place of RocksDB, set Options::nvm_setup (a shared_ptr<NvmSetup> with use_nvm_module, pmem_path and L0 size thresholds), and levels L1 and below stay ordinary SSTables on the SSD.
how_it_is_fast: Flushed MemTables are written to NVM as sorted 'RowTables' in a matrix container. When the receiver half fills up it becomes the compactor, and its data is merged into L1 by column compaction: one small key range at a time, taken across all RowTables and matched with the overlapping L1 SSTables, rather than all of L0 against all of L1. In the paper this meant 467 compactions of about 0.33 GB each, versus RocksDB's 52 compactions averaging 3.1 GB. Because a column's cost does not grow with level width, L1 is widened to 8 GB, which flattens the tree from 5 levels to 3 and lowers write amplification. Cross-row hint search stores a forward pointer from each key into the previous RowTable, in the style of fractional cascading, so point lookups in the large unsorted L0 need no Bloom filters.
when_to_use: Sustained random-insert or update-heavy workloads (bulk load, YCSB load/A/F-like) where RocksDB's L0-L1 compaction stalls cause throughput troughs and p99/p99.9 spikes.

You already have Optane DC PMM (or equivalent byte-addressable persistent memory mounted for PMDK), several GB of it free, and a comparatively slow SSD for the lower levels (the paper's SSD managed 68 MB/s for 4 KB random writes).
Any value size from 64 B to 64 KB, since the paper's random-write gain over RocksDB with L0 on NVM was 1.86-3.61x across that whole range (3.6x at 4 KB).
Research or prototyping: reproducing the ATC'20 results, or as a reference design for column compaction and cross-row L0 search when adding a persistent-memory tier to an LSM engine.
when_not_to_use: Machines without persistent memory. Intel wound down Optane in July 2022, so new deployments need other hardware, and pmem_map_file's msync fallback on an ordinary file is not the configuration that was measured.
Read- or scan-dominated workloads. In the paper, random and sequential reads roughly matched RocksDB and YCSB B-E were only 'adequate'. An open issue (#3) reports high read latency under YCSB-C++.
Sequential-insert workloads. In the paper, stock RocksDB on SSD beat every NVM variant, MatrixKV included, on sequential writes.

Production systems. The code is frozen at RocksDB 5.18.3 with none of RocksDB's later fixes. Issues about NVM overuse and a crash when freed L0 space was not reclaimed (#2) have had no answer since 2021, and debug logging is compiled in.
Many column families on a small NVM device, because each named column family maps its own pool file sized from the L0 stop threshold.

integration.form: static lib (the whole RocksDB v5.18.3 tree plus utilities/nvm_mod, built with the Makefile; the README says CMake is not supported)
integration.dependencies: PMDK libpmem (Makefile links -lpmem), pthread; RocksDB's usual optional compression libraries (snappy, lz4, zstd) if present
integration.min_toolchain: C++11 (build_detect_platform and the Makefile force -std=c++11); the paper used Fedora 27 / Linux 4.13.9; the compiler version is not documented
integration.platforms: Linux with PMDK and a DAX-mounted persistent-memory path (tested on x86-64 with Optane DC PMM); other platforms not documented
integration.thread_safety: Follows RocksDB 5.18's DB-handle model. MatrixKV's NVM flush jobs assert the DB mutex is held, and sstable_meta.h notes that its compaction file list is used by only one thread; nothing further is documented. Neither the paper nor the issues state the benchmark thread count (issue #4), and the shipped db_bench script uses threads=1.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: same RocksDB 5.18 C++ API and db_bench, but you must replace your RocksDB build with this fork (it is not a plugin), give up every RocksDB feature and fix after 5.18.3, and configure nvm_setup plus a pmem path; L0 data lives in a pool file outside the DB directory

gotchas: NVM footprint is much larger than the 8 GB L0 budget. Master pre-allocates (L0_stop_size / write_buffer_size + 1) * 2 slots of write_buffer_size + 8 MB each, about 18.6 GB with the defaults (8 GB stop, 64 MB memtables), which fits issue #2's report of nearly 20 GB. The page-granular space management described in the paper exists only on the unmerged MatrixKV-Pager branch, which uses 256 KB pages rather than 4 KB.

The paper's full speedup depends on also flattening the tree. The shipped script sets max_bytes_for_level_base to 8 GB; with RocksDB's default 256 MB L1 you get only the write-stall reduction, and the paper reports 25% more throughput with the 8 GB L1. L0 thresholds are byte sizes (7 GB trigger, 7.5 GB slowdown, 8 GB stop by default) instead of RocksDB's file counts.

Recovery is fragile. If the pmem pool file is missing while the manifest still lists L0 files, RecoverFromStorageInfo prints 'can't recover' and carries on. It also copies each L0 table's key metadata into a stack variable-length array, which could overflow the thread stack for small-value tables. A RowTable flush returns IOError if its data plus about 52 bytes of metadata per key (with 16 B keys) exceeds its fixed slot.

Debug logging is hard-wired: my_log.h defines LZW_DEBUG and LZW_INFO, so the library appends to NVM_LOG in the working directory, opening and closing the file for every line, on each L0 table add or delete and each column-compaction pick. The paper says the WAL lives on NVM, but the shipped script puts --wal_dir on the SSD, and utilities/nvm_mod contains no WAL code.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick MatrixKV only when you have Optane-class persistent memory and the problem is RocksDB write stalls and tail latency under random inserts. It is the only sibling built for a DRAM/NVM/SSD hierarchy, and in the paper's all-NVM comparison it led while PebblesDB gained little over RocksDB. On plain SSDs, SplinterDB, KVell or PebblesDB are the write-throughput alternatives, and Titan is the maintained plug-in choice if your problem is large values.
verified_claims_summary: In the USENIX ATC'20 paper's db_bench test (80 GB of 16 B-key / 4 KB-value inserts in uniform random order, RocksDB defaults, 8 GB of NVM per store), MatrixKV reached 3.6x the random-write throughput of RocksDB with an 8 GB L0 placed in Optane (1.86-3.61x across 64 B-64 KB values) and 2.6x NoveLSM, and 3.29x on YCSB load. YCSB-A p99 at about 20K req/s was 405 us, against 786 us for RocksDB-L0-NVM, 2,080 us for NoveLSM and 11,055 us for stock RocksDB on SSD, and SSD write amplification was 3.43x versus 8.78x for stock RocksDB. Hardware: two unnamed 24-core 2.2 GHz Intel CPUs, 32 GB DRAM, an Intel SSDSC2BB800G7 SSD and Optane DC PMM on Fedora 27 / Linux 4.13.9; compiler, flags and client thread count are not stated.
status_note: Abandoned since August 2020 (3 open issues with no maintainer replies) and tied to discontinued Optane hardware. The code inherits RocksDB's GPLv2 / Apache-2.0 dual license and is best treated as a vendorable research reference for its column-compaction and L0-search design, not as a production engine.
